text:
Newbury's Coral Gold Cup: Jamie Lynch's horse-by-horse guide to Saturday's feature handicap chase live on Sky Sports Racing
Ahead of the big Coral Gold Cup showdown on Saturday, Sky Sports Racing's senior form analyst Jamie Lynch offers his verdict on every runner going to post in search of top honours; watch the race at 3pm on Saturday - LIVE on Sky Sports Racing
Wednesday 25 November 2026 17:16, UK
Jamie Lynch assesses the confirmations and reveals his top tip for one of the most prestigious handicaps of the season this Saturday, live on Sky Sports Racing.
The Coral Gold Cup at Newbury at 3pm is one of the biggest and best handicap chases of the entire season, although conditions will be a break from the norm - the reason the race is a little lighter at the top end this time, with only one rated above 150.
But there is the usual stack of classy second-season chasers with high trajectories and higher aspirations, meaning that - as always - it's going to take a lot of winning. Let's look at all those entered for this high-prestige prize, just one part of a stellar Saturday on Sky Sports Racing.
Watch every race of the Coral Gold Cup meeting from Newbury live on Sky Sports Racing on Friday 27th and Saturday 28th November.

- Grey Dawning oozes class in Betfair Chase repeat
Three Card Brag
Trainer: Gordon Elliott
He ran the race of his life when beating all bar Panic Attack in last year's renewal, conceding weight all round, the same again here, but he hasn't reproduced that level since, though one race was the Grand National and the latest smacked of a prep run, off a break and ridden by a 7lb conditional jockey.
The last top-weight winner was the daddy, Denman, whose mark was 20lb higher, if you don't mind.
King Alexander
Trainer: Willie Mullins
Has had the privilege of residing at two of the finest horseracing hotels in history, trained firstly by Nicky Henderson and then Willie Mullins, for whom he won the Galway Plate in July against the odds, as the outsider of the stable's four.
That has left him with what's probably too high a mark now, so says the Kerry National in which he finished an unthreatening sixth.
Regent's Stroll
Trainer: Paul Nicholls
A nephew of the legendary Denman, who had a mark of 161 when he made a successful reappearance in this race in his second season over fences, Regent's Stroll is not quite on the same trajectory but ended his novice campaign on a high at the Festivals. He was third at Cheltenham to Meetmebythesea and Gold Dancer in the Jack Richards and second to the latter in the Mildmay.
We haven't seen all he's got, including for stamina, and the stable can still get one primed and readied for this, highlighted by Kandoo Kid in 2024. Big chance.
Downmexicoway
Trainer: Henry de Bromhead
He was third in the Kerry National last time where his status as favourite spoke of his developing talent, having caught the eye in the Plates at both Cheltenham and Galway. Being a second-season chaser from the Henry de Bromhead yard is reason enough to put him on a shortlist, and then there are the added bonuses of his untapped stamina and suitability to non-November ground.
Wendigo
Trainer: Jamie Snowden
The classic profile for this race, as a second-season chaser with a touch of class and an eye on the biggest staying prizes: the most memorable winners of the Hennessy, now the Coral Gold Cup, have all had a look of Wendigo. He was rated 147 following his third to Kitzbuhel in the Kauto Star almost a year ago, and he's still rated that now, perhaps generously so.
The signs from his reappearance were loud and clear that he's an improved model, to give 10lb to Potters Charm and a heavy beating to Doyen Quest at Carlisle, all without the need to play his ace card, the stamina card. If you tasked AI with creating a Coral Gold Cup winner, the technical drawings would be of Wendigo.
Masaccio
Trainer: Alan King
This horse missed the whole of last season, not that anybody could have told from his finding, grinding comeback win - at odds of 33/1 - in a 16-runner handicap hurdle at Newbury, like he'd never been away.
As a novice chaser, he was second to The Jukebox Man in the Grade Two John Francome in 2024, as well as third to Jagwar in the Plate at the Cheltenham Festival. That form makes a mark of 147 well within reach, though the 'bounce' factor is obviously high with him.
Panic Attack
Trainer: Dan Skelton
The heroine of last year, but she was coming in hot then, unlike now, absent since April. Also, she's 6lb higher now, or effectively 9lb considering that Tristan Durrell claimed 3lb back then.
History tells us how hard a repeat is - Arkle being the only one to ever do it in back-to-back years.
Miami Magic
Trainer: Stuart Edmunds
Stuart Edmunds' charge was classy but clumsy as a novice chaser, exemplified by the Mildmay at Aintree, where he went off 7/2 and looked a threat when he came down at the fourth-last. Only Masaccio prevented the perfect prep in a hurdle at Newbury, and Miami Magic has got the game to win a race like this.
He's unbothered by drying ground, but there are 21 fences and almost as many rivals in his way, an unforgiving environment for a sketchy jumper.
Holloway Queen
Trainer: Nicky Henderson
A magical metamorphosis through last season, which started with a PU and a UR and ended in two 'wow' wins, culminating with the National Hunt Chase.
A 10lb hit requires her to pick up where she left off and then some, and the unseasonable autumn has impeded her traditional stable more than most, raising some doubt as to whether she'll be razor sharp first time out.
The Jukebox Kid
Trainer: Willie Mullins
The small print reads differently to Regent's Stroll and Wendigo but the formula fabric is still the same, as a second-season chaser from a leading yard. His reappearance over hurdles was a means to an end, not much in the way of bite even so, after a summer wind op, and this track is very different to right-handed Ascot where he's looked most at home as a chaser.
Myretown
Trainers: Lucinda Russell and Michael Scudamore
This contender fell when favourite for this 12 months ago, the omen for a season which was essentially a write-off. But, with the reset button pressed over the summer, he was back looking more the Myretown of old in dismissing a trio of inferior rivals at Kelso, a confidence-restoring exercise, as well as a greater connecting point back to his showstopper in the 2025 Ultima. That was the reason he topped the market last year off the same mark as now.
Road To Home
Trainer: Willie Mullins
Got better as a novice and showed he can cut it in big-field handicaps with his placings in the Kim Muir and the bet365 Gold Cup, beaten a neck in one and a neck and a short-head in the other. Won a mere maiden chase on his return at Galway but was as big as 9/2 that day, on account of the trip (an inadequate 2m 2f), putting him ahead of schedule for his primary target, at a track that plugs into his properties.
Amirite
Trainer: Chris Gordon
In his time with Henry de Bromhead, he was 0/6 with his British raids, including pulling up in the latest Grand National at 100/1, and his first start for Chris Gordon amounted to little, albeit over hurdles and without the usual tongue tie.
Havaila
Trainer: Jamie and Josh Moore
Seems a lot older than seven, largely because he's high mileage (began with Sir Michael Stoute), which made his spring surge all the more remarkable, not returning until January but improving 25lb and bringing up the hat-trick in the bet365 Gold Cup. As a late bloomer with a come-from-behind style, his ceiling isn't so discernible as many in here.
The Doyen Chief
Trainer: Nick Scholfield
The chief sufferer in the chaotic start when 14/1 for this last year (trained by Alan King), which was more of a window of opportunity for him than this renewal, having lost a bit of lustre in the meantime, for all that his first start for Nick Scholfield when runner-up at Market Rasen suggested that most of his ability was intact.
Booster Bob
Trainer: Olly Murphy
Two for two in handicap chases at Newbury, the first all down to Sean Bowen (having traded at 880/1 in-running) and the second coming on his reappearance on this very day last year, in the 2m 6f event. The rest of the campaign was a bit of a washout but who knows what he can do at this sort of trip, back fresh and back at Newbury? He's something of a mystery box.
One Big Bang
Trainer: James Owen
Thrived in big fields as a hurdler, and his first experience of such a scenario as a chaser prompted a fine third in the National Hunt Chase, after which he was excusably overwhelmed in the Irish National. Another to use the staying hurdle here earlier in the month as a stepping stone to this, and his component parts qualify him as a lively longshot, in the same way his dam's half-brother Madison Du Berlais was when he won this at 25/1 in 2008.
Kap Vert
Trainer: Philip Hobbs and Johnson White
Some going and some stamina to win the Scottish National as a novice, on ground that was officially heavy. But he's not one dimensional, nor maxed out, based on an encouraging return at Aintree, and he's only a six-year-old. A field, or a jumping test, such as this holds no fears for him.
Mr Hope Street
Trainer: Dan Skelton
His success in a high-value handicap at Aintree on National day is the one and only time he's tackled 3m+ over fences, no coincidence in that, nor the fact he has saved his second go for this, after a screw-tightening reappearance over 2m 4f at Stratford. This perceptible plan, and the man orchestrating it (Dan Skelton), are big selling points.
Here Comes Georgie
Trainer: Dan Skelton
This contender started with a bang for Skelton at Cheltenham and perhaps had a hangover from that when underwhelming at Aintree a fortnight later. He's in a similar boat but not the same mould as Panic Attack from last year.
JAMIE LYNCH'S VERDICT
The likes of Wendigo and Regent's Stroll speak for themselves, both a profiler's dream for this race, but, for that very reason, the market is giving nothing away for either. The ill-fated Gold Dancer beat both in the Mildmay, and his form is tied in with DOWNMEXICOWAY, who has got in some valuable practice for big-field handicaps while continually hinting at better to come.
